newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Jews recall Bulgaria's WWII refusal to deport them.
newsitem.headline: Jews recall Bulgaria's WWII refusal to deport them.

text.p: Members of Bulgaria's Jewish community on Sunday commemorated those who helped save them from deportation and death at the hands of the Nazis during World War Two.

On March 9, 1943, a delegation of five Bulgarians from Kyustendil, led by the speaker of parliament Dimitar Peshev, came to Sofia to appeal against the deportations ordered by Bulgaria's wartime ally Germany.

A storm of protest against any deportation of Bulgaria's 50,000 Jews, from parliamentarians, the Orthodox Church and Bulgarian society as a whole helped give King Boris III grounds to resist the German pressure.

"Bulgarian Jews have been living in this country for centuries. They have contributed much to the development of Bulgarian culture and have never constituted any threat to the Bulgarian state," Vice-President Todor Kavaldzhiev told Sunday's ceremony near the site of Kyustendil's old synagogue.
"We should not look on their salvation as some superhuman deed but as ordinary humanity."
Bulgarian Jews had to wear Star of David badges, many businesses and professions were forbidden them and men were drafted to build roads, but none died in the Nazi death camps.

On Friday, President Petar Stoyanov ordered that Peshev's delegation of three parliamentary deputies and two other public figures who first warned of the deportations should be posthumously awarded the Order of Stara Planina, first class.

Peshev was jailed by the communists after the war and his property was seized. Vladimir Kourtev, a member of the Macedonian nationalist IMRO organisation, was summoned by the interior minister in 1946 and never seen again.
Almost all Bulgaria's Jews emigrated to Israel after World War Two, and now the community numbers no more than 7,000.

Most Bulgarian Jews are Sephardic, descendents of the Jews forced out of Spain in 1492. They were invited by the Ottomans, who offered religious freedom in exchange for the practice of their skills as artisans and merchants.

Under communist rule until 1989, credit for saving the Jews was given to the communist partisans. Yaakov Djerassi, president of the Zion Jewish committee, told Reuters the role of the king, who died in unexplained circumstances in August 1943, had only recently begun to win more recognition.
"The royal family never sought any credit for what they did," Djerassi said.

Sofia's synagogue was reopened last September and its choir performed on Sunday. First inaugurated in 1909, it was hit by a bomb during World War Two and restoration was forbidden by the communist government until its fall in 1989.

Djerassi told Sunday's ceremony, which was also attended by representatives of the Orthodox Church, that Bulgaria's saving of its Jewish community deserved more international recognition, particularly now as the country struggled with severe economic crisis.
"We have to remember that it was not (former communist leader) Todor Zhivkov or the communists that saved the Jews, it was the people of Kyustendil," he said.
"The whole world should know there is a noble nation in the heart of Europe and should remember this country now when it is in need."
